findings.english_quote: The two accusatives κἀκεῖνον and αὐτόν appear to refer to the same person, producing a redundant or resumptive construction. The translation provisionally treats αὐτόν as emphatic (“that man himself”); alternatively, one pronoun may be secondary.
findings.issue: The emphatic/resumptive main rendering is defensible, but the note omits a materially different grammatical analysis: κἀκεῖνον can be the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι, while αὐτόν is the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, contextually referring to Clement from the requesting participants’ perspective. The presence of two accusatives therefore does not itself establish redundancy or support deleting one. This is an interpretive disclosure problem, not an established source-corruption block.
findings.suggested_revision: Explain both the emphatic/resumptive interpretation and the subject–object interpretation, including the person shift involved in the latter. Remove the proposed deletion unless it is separately supported and explicitly identified as a conjecture. A source-transparent English candidate for fresh review is “and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well.”

findings.source_quote: οὐ μόνον αὐτῆς τυχεῖν ἡγούμην ἀδύνατον εἶναι, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ προσαγορεῦσαί ποτε ἤλπιζον
findings.english_quote: I considered it impossible not only to obtain her, but I never even hoped to address her.
findings.issue: The English places “not only” inside the infinitival complement of “impossible,” but then pairs it with an independent finite clause. This defective coordination obscures the Greek’s escalation: not only did Appion judge obtaining her impossible; he did not even hope ever to address her. Both negative claims remain present, but their grammatical relationship needs correction.
findings.suggested_revision: For fresh review: “Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her.”
